question: Studies cited in the handbook show that most crash-involved riders make which braking mistake?
choice_a: They underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear
choice_b: They brake too far in advance of a hazard
choice_c: They use only the front brake
explanation: Studies show that most crash-involved riders underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear, or fail to separate braking from swerving.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.26, 'Crash Avoidance'

question: To stop quickly, the handbook says you should:
choice_b: Apply both brakes at the same time, squeezing the front brake lever firmly and progressively
choice_d: Coast to a stop without braking at all
explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time; squeeze the brake lever firmly and progressively, and press down on the rear brake.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.26, 'Quick Stops'

question: If the front wheel locks while braking, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Continue holding the front brake locked
choice_b: Immediately apply full rear brake instead
choice_c: Release the front brake immediately, then reapply it firmly
choice_d: Let go of both brakes and coast to a stop
explanation: If the front wheel locks, release the front brake immediately, then reapply it firmly.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.26, 'Quick Stops'

question: If you accidentally lock the rear wheel on a good traction surface, the handbook says you should:
choice_a: Release it and reapply it repeatedly
choice_b: Immediately release the rear brake and rely only on the front
choice_c: Swerve to try to break the skid
choice_d: Keep it locked until you have completely stopped, as long as the motorcycle is upright and going straight
explanation: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, keep it locked until completely stopped; you can control the motorcycle on a straightaway if it is upright and straight.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.26, 'Quick Stops'

question: According to the handbook, the front brake can provide how much of a motorcycle's potential stopping power?
choice_c: None; it is for steering assistance only
explanation: Always use both brakes at the same time to stop -- the front brake can provide 70% or more of the potential stopping power.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.27, 'Quick Stops'

question: If you must stop quickly while turning or riding a curve, the best technique according to the handbook is to:
choice_a: Brake hard immediately while still leaning
choice_b: Straighten the motorcycle upright first, then brake
choice_c: Release the throttle only, without using the brakes
choice_d: Swerve first, then brake while still leaning
explanation: If you must stop quickly while turning or riding a curve, the best technique is to straighten the bike upright first and then brake.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.27, 'Quick Stops'

question: If you cannot straighten the motorcycle before stopping in a curve, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Apply maximum brake pressure immediately, regardless of lean angle
choice_b: Release the brakes entirely until the curve ends
choice_c: Apply light brakes and reduce the throttle, increasing brake pressure as you reduce your lean angle
choice_d: Accelerate through the curve instead of braking
explanation: If you must brake while leaning, apply light brakes and reduce the throttle; as you slow, reduce your lean angle and apply more brake pressure until the motorcycle is straight.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.27, 'Quick Stops'

question: The handbook describes a swerve as:
choice_a: A gradual, wide turn taken well before an obstacle
choice_b: A complete stop followed by a U-turn
choice_c: A maneuver used only at very low speed
choice_d: Any sudden change in direction, such as two quick turns or a rapid shift to the side
explanation: A swerve is any sudden change in direction -- it can be two quick turns, or a rapid shift to the side.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.27, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: To swerve, the handbook says you should apply hand pressure to the handlegrip:
choice_a: On the side of your intended direction of escape
choice_b: On the side opposite your intended direction of escape
choice_c: On both handlegrips equally at the same time
choice_d: Only after you have already passed the obstacle
explanation: Apply a small amount of hand pressure to the handlegrip located on the side of your intended direction of escape; this causes the motorcycle to lean quickly.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.27, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: While swerving, the handbook advises you to keep your body:
choice_a: Leaning further over than the motorcycle itself
choice_b: Upright, while allowing the motorcycle to lean underneath you
choice_c: Rigid and locked against the handlebars
choice_d: Tucked down flat against the gas tank
explanation: Keep your body upright and allow the motorcycle to lean in the direction of the turn, keeping your knees against the tank and feet on the pegs.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.27, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: To swerve to the left and then recover your original direction of travel, the handbook says you should:
choice_a: Press the right handlegrip, then press the left to recover
choice_b: Press both handlegrips at the same time
choice_c: Press the left handlegrip, then press the right to recover
choice_d: Pull back on the throttle only, without steering input
explanation: To swerve to the left, press the left handlegrip, then press the right to recover; to swerve right, press right, then left.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.27-28, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: Regarding braking and swerving together, what rule does the handbook give?
choice_a: Always brake and swerve at the exact same instant
choice_b: Braking and swerving should never both be used in the same emergency
choice_c: Swerving automatically applies the rear brake for you
choice_d: Separate them -- brake before or after, but never while swerving
explanation: If braking is required, separate it from swerving. Brake before or after -- never while swerving.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.28, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: A primary cause of single-vehicle motorcycle crashes, according to the handbook, is:
choice_a: Running wide in a curve or turn and colliding with the roadway or a fixed object
choice_b: Following at too great a distance
choice_d: Riding with the headlight on during the day
explanation: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn and colliding with the roadway or a fixed object.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.28, 'Cornering'

question: Regarding the ideal path through a curve, the handbook notes that:
choice_a: You must always follow the exact geometric center of the lane
choice_b: Your best path may not always follow the curve of the road
choice_c: You should always hug the inside edge of a curve from entry to exit
choice_d: Speed should always increase through the middle of every curve
explanation: Your best path may not always follow the curve of the road; change lane position depending on traffic, road conditions, and the curve itself.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.28-29, 'Cornering'

question: If no other traffic is present, one cornering technique described in the handbook is to:
choice_a: Ride the inside edge of the curve for its entire length
choice_b: Ride the outside edge of the curve for its entire length
choice_c: Start at the outside of the curve, move toward the inside near the center, then move back outside to exit
choice_d: Change lanes repeatedly throughout the curve
explanation: If no traffic is present, start at the outside of a curve to increase your line of sight and the effective radius of the turn, moving toward the inside as you pass the center, then back outside to exit.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.29, 'Cornering'

question: Staying in the center of your lane throughout a curve, as an alternative technique, is useful because it:
choice_a: Is the only lane position permitted by law while cornering
choice_b: Automatically raises the effective speed limit through the curve
choice_c: Eliminates the need for any head checks
choice_d: Lets you spot approaching traffic sooner and adjust for center-line crowding or debris
explanation: Another alternative is to stay in the center of your lane throughout the curve, permitting you to spot approaching traffic sooner and adjust for crowding or debris.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.29, 'Cornering'
